pages.title: Al-Andalus and Its Place in Spain
pages.content:
Muslims ruled over a large part of the Iberian Peninsula, present-day Spain and Portugal, from 711 to 1492. The lands under Muslim rule were known as Al-Andalus. Although the territory under their control shrank steadily after the 11th century, the Muslim presence lasted there for 781 years until only the Kingdom of Granada (Gırnata Sultanlığı) remained. Particularly during the first three centuries, they established the most advanced and brilliant civilization the West had ever seen. Above all, they produced numerous invaluable works in art and architecture, as well as in other fields like medicine, literature, and philosophy.

The region, which includes major cities of the era such as Granada (Gırnata), Sevilla (İşbiliye), and Córdoba (Kurtuba), is today one of Spain’s 17 autonomous communities and is known as “Andalusia/Endülüs.”

vocabulary.definition: Land that a ruler or a state controls.
Extremely useful; too valuable to measure.
Governing itself, with its own local government.

exercises.title: A Long Presence
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: Which statement best summarizes Chapter 1?
options: Muslim rule lasted 781 years and produced invaluable works, even though its territory shrank.
Muslim rule grew stronger every century until 1492.
Al-Andalus was a small region that produced little art or science.

feedback.correct: Correct. A long presence, a shrinking territory and a rich legacy.
feedback.incorrect: Read the first paragraph again. Look for although and Above all.

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: Although and the Unexpected
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what the although-clause does.
languageFocusExercises.question: “Although the territory under their control shrank steadily after the 11th century, the Muslim presence lasted there for 781 years.” What does the although-clause do?
options: It gives a fact that makes the main clause surprising.
It gives the reason why the presence lasted so long.
It describes what happened after 781 years.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: An although-clause states a fact that would normally lead us to expect the opposite of the main clause. The shrinking territory makes the 781 years of presence more remarkable.

feedback.correct: Yes. The although-clause sets up a contrast with the main clause.
feedback.incorrect: Would a shrinking territory normally make a long presence more or less likely?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Which, As Well As, Ever
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from Chapter 1.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form completes the sentence correctly?

formChoices.sentence: The region, [choice] includes major cities of the era such as Granada, Sevilla, and Córdoba, is today one of Spain’s 17 autonomous communities.
They produced numerous invaluable works in art and architecture, [choice] in other fields like medicine.
They established the most advanced and brilliant civilization the West [choice] seen.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A non-defining clause between commas uses which, never that. “As well as” adds a further area. “Had ever seen” looks back from a past point: no earlier civilization in the West was as advanced.

feedback.correct: Well done. Which, as well as, had ever.
feedback.incorrect: Check the commas, the meaning of addition, and the time we look back from.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Reformulate the Facts
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How else can the same facts be expressed?

transformItems.source: Although the territory shrank steadily, the Muslim presence lasted for 781 years.
transformItems.frame: Despite the territory [blank] steadily, the Muslim presence lasted for 781 years.

transformItems.source: They established the most advanced civilization the West had ever seen.
transformItems.frame: The West had never seen [blank] advanced civilization.

transformItems.source: The lands under Muslim rule were known as Al-Andalus.
transformItems.frame: People [blank] the lands under Muslim rule Al-Andalus.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Although + clause” can become “despite + noun + -ing”. A superlative with “ever” can become “never … such a(n) …”. A passive “were known as” can become active with “people called …”.

feedback.correct: Correct. The meaning stays the same in a new structure.
feedback.incorrect: Use despite + -ing, never … such an, and an active verb.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: A Region and Its Heritage
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences about a region with a long history.
languageFocusExercises.question: How has its past shaped what it is today?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “Konya, which was the capital of the Anatolian Seljuks, is today one of Türkiye’s largest cities. Although it lies far from the sea, it was an important center of trade for centuries. It produced famous works of architecture as well as great scholars and poets. Its madrasas and mosques still attract many visitors. In this way, its past continues to shape its identity.”

feedback.correct: Check: a non-defining clause with which, although, as well as and a clear concluding sentence.

discussionPrompts.question: Introduce the region with a non-defining relative clause.
discussionPrompts.example: Konya, which was the Seljuk capital, …

pages.title: The Beginning of Muslim Spain
pages.content:
The history of Muslim Spain dates back to the early eighth century in the western Mediterranean region, where Europe and Africa almost meet. The Muslim conquerors who came here from Syria, Arabia, and Egypt were determined soldiers driven by a strong belief. In 711, Târık b. Ziyâd, the Berber (Berberî: a people who live in North Africa) governor of Tangier (Tanca: a historic city in northwestern Morocco), started the conquest of the Iberian Peninsula with an army which was made up mostly of Berbers. (Iberian Peninsula is a large peninsula located in southwestern Europe that today covers the countries of Spain and Portugal.) Târık b. Ziyâd captured the Visigothic capital of Toledo in 711. One year later, in 712, the Umayyad (Emevi) governor of Ifriqiya (roughly present-day Tunisia, eastern Algeria and western Libya) Mûsâ b. Nusayr, joined him. Then, the two commanders led a fast military campaign and completed the conquest of most of the peninsula within three years.

At that time, the Visigothic Kingdom that ruled Spain was having a hard time dealing with various problems caused by internal conflicts over the throne, social unrest, and the policy of forcing Jews to become Christians. It is known that during the conquest, the people of some cities who were dissatisfied with Visigothic rule, particularly the Jews, voluntarily opened their gates to the Muslims. During those years, the villagers were really living a hard life. Most of the people viewed Muslims as saviors and cooperated with them. As some historians say, “Spain, which was conquered so easily by the Muslims, suffered from grave internal weaknesses.”

vocabulary.definition: Began at a particular time in the past.
Having a strong wish to do something and not giving up.
Taking control of a land by force.
Formed by a number of people or things.
Took control of a place by force.
Fights between groups inside the same country.
Angry protests and disorder among people.
People who save others from danger.

exercises.question: Why was the conquest so fast?

items: determined soldiers driven by a strong belief
a fast military campaign led by two commanders
internal conflicts over the throne
social unrest
the policy of forcing Jews to become Christians

The conquerors: determined soldiers driven by a strong belief
a fast military campaign led by two commanders

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: Driven By, Caused By
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what “driven by” replaces.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: A past participle clause (driven by …) is a shorter form of a passive relative clause (who were driven by …). Academic history texts use it to pack information into one sentence.

feedback.incorrect: Who was driven, and by what?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Reporting Facts and Views
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from Chapter 2.
languageFocusExercises.question: How does the writer report facts and views?

[choice] some historians say, “Spain suffered from grave internal weaknesses.”
The Visigothic Kingdom was having a hard time [choice] with various problems.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It is known that …” presents a generally accepted fact. “As some historians say, …” attributes a view to a source. “Have a hard time + -ing” describes difficulty.

feedback.correct: Well done. It is known, As, dealing.
feedback.incorrect: Check the impersonal passive, the reporting word and the verb form after “a hard time”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Reduce the Clause
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence with a participle clause. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can a relative clause be shortened?

transformItems.source: Târık started the conquest with an army which was made up mostly of Berbers.

transformItems.source: The people who were dissatisfied with Visigothic rule opened their gates.
transformItems.frame: The people [blank] with Visigothic rule opened their gates.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: When a relative clause has “which/who + be + past participle or adjective”, we can drop “which/who + be”: an army made up of …, problems caused by …, people dissatisfied with …

feedback.correct: Correct. You reduced each clause.
feedback.incorrect: Drop “which was”, “were” and “who were”.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: Explaining a Fast Change
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences explaining why a change happened quickly.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which internal and external causes can you give?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “Our school moved to online lessons within two weeks. It is known that many schools found this difficult. However, our teachers, supported by a small IT team, prepared the lessons quickly. Students, already familiar with the platform, joined without problems. As some parents say, the main reason was good planning. The change was fast because the school was ready.”

feedback.correct: Check: a participle clause, It is known that, a reported view and a clear cause.

discussionPrompts.question: Describe the change in one sentence.
discussionPrompts.example: Our school moved to digital lessons in a few weeks.

discussionPrompts.question: Give an internal cause with a participle clause.
discussionPrompts.example: Teachers, supported by the IT team, …

discussionPrompts.question: Attribute one view with “As … say,”.
discussionPrompts.example: As some parents say, …

options: Their people were dissatisfied with Visigothic rule.

I can analyze the internal causes that made the conquest easy.
I can use participle clauses, “It is known that” and reported views.

pages.title: A Golden Age of Culture
pages.content:
During the time when the famous Andalusian traveler Ibn Jubayr was born (1145, Valencia), culture in Muslim Spain was in its golden age. Among the region’s renowned thinkers were the Sufi philosopher and writer Ibn al-Arabi (1165–1240), the scientist and philosopher Ibn Rushd (1126–1198) and philosopher and physician Ibn Tufayl (1105-1185). At that time, Granada possessed a higher level of civilization than most cities further east. During the same period, Sevilla had 500 bathhouses and 1,000 mosques. Córdoba, with a population of between 300,000 to 500,000, was the largest city in Western Europe. The level of civilization impressed medieval Christians. As some historians have pointed out, Islamic Spain, with its material and intellectual elements of higher culture, stood out against the barrenness of contemporary life in the rest of Western Europe.

The civilization in Al-Andalus, which was shaped by the mixture of European, Asian, and African cultural elements, has a distinct and strong character that sets it apart from other regions of the Islamic world. Indeed, the influence of eight centuries of Islamic rule in the region continued even after Christians retook the region.

In this region, not only did different cultures come together, but two distinct socioeconomic systems also came into contact. The first was the urban Islamic bloc, which conducted commercial activities within an economic network linked to the Mediterranean and beyond the Islamic world and operated a monetary economy. The second was the Christian bloc, an agricultural society dominated by rural life.

Moreover, with the conquest, the Mediterranean Sea, known as the “Roman Lake”, was transformed from a closed sea into a global trade route connected to the Indian Ocean.

vocabulary.definition: Said something to draw attention to it.
A lack of life, ideas or growth.
Belonging to the same period of time.
Mainly controlled or shaped by something.

hotspots.description: Ibn al-Arabi, Ibn Rushd and Ibn Tufayl lived in Al-Andalus during its cultural golden age.

hotspots.title: The Roman Lake

exercises.title: Two Systems
exercises.instructions: Sort each feature into the right bloc.
exercises.question: How were the two systems different?

items: urban
commercial activities linked to the Mediterranean
a monetary economy
agricultural
dominated by rural life

The Islamic bloc: commercial activities linked to the Mediterranean

exercises.explanation: Chapter 3: “The first was the urban Islamic bloc, which conducted commercial activities … and operated a monetary economy. The second was the Christian bloc, an agricultural society dominated by rural life.”

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: Not Only Did …
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what is special about its word order.
languageFocusExercises.question: “In this region, not only did different cultures come together, but two distinct socioeconomic systems also came into contact.” What is special here?
options: After “not only” at the start, the auxiliary comes before the subject.
The verb comes at the end of the sentence.
There is no subject in the first part.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: When a negative or limiting phrase such as “not only” starts a clause, English uses question word order (inversion): not only did different cultures come together. This adds emphasis in formal writing.

feedback.correct: Correct. “Did” comes before “different cultures”.
feedback.incorrect: Compare it with: Different cultures came together.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Comparing Levels
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which comparative form fits?

formChoices.sentence: Granada possessed a [choice] level of civilization than most cities further east.
Córdoba was the [choice] city in Western Europe.
Islamic Spain stood out [choice] the barrenness of contemporary life in the rest of Western Europe.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: Use a comparative with than and a superlative with the. “Stand out against” presents something clearly different from its background.

feedback.correct: Well done. Higher, largest, against.
feedback.incorrect: Is there “than” or “the”? Which preposition follows “stood out”?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Add Emphasis with Inversion
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Rewrite each sentence with the words given. Keep the meaning.
languageFocusExercises.question: How can we add emphasis?

transformItems.source: Different cultures came together, and two systems also came into contact.
transformItems.frame: Not only [blank] different cultures come together, but two systems also came into contact.

transformItems.source: Sevilla had 500 bathhouses, and it also had 1,000 mosques.
transformItems.frame: Not only [blank] Sevilla have 500 bathhouses, but it also had 1,000 mosques.

transformItems.source: The civilization has a distinct character that makes it different from other regions.
transformItems.frame: The civilization has a distinct character that [blank] it apart from other regions.

languageFocusExercises.explanation: “Not only + auxiliary + subject + verb …, but … also …” adds emphasis. “Set something apart from” = make it different from.

feedback.correct: Correct. You used inversion and “sets apart”.
feedback.incorrect: Put did before the subject after Not only.

languageFocusExercises.title: Use: What Makes a Golden Age?
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Write a paragraph of six to eight sentences about what makes a place or period a “golden age”.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which evidence would you use?
languageFocusExercises.explanation: Example: “A golden age is a period when a society reaches a high level in science, art and daily life. Al-Andalus in the 12th century is a good example. Not only did it produce great thinkers, but it also had large, well-organized cities. Córdoba was the largest city in Western Europe. Compared with other cities of the time, it was far more developed. Such evidence shows why historians call it a golden age.”

feedback.correct: Check: a definition, one inversion, one comparison and evidence from the text.

discussionPrompts.question: Give your definition of a golden age.
discussionPrompts.example: A golden age is a period when …

discussionPrompts.question: Use “not only … but also” with inversion.
discussionPrompts.example: Not only did the city have …, but it also …

discussionPrompts.question: Compare it with another place or time.
discussionPrompts.example: Compared with …, it was far more …

beforeYouRead.question: Find it fast: What was the largest city in Western Europe?
beforeYouRead.quote: Córdoba, with a population of between 300,000 to 500,000, was the largest city in Western Europe.

I can compare the two socioeconomic systems that came into contact.

pages.title: The Umayyad State in Al-Andalus
pages.content:
The conquest of Al-Andalus marks the final stage of the early Islamic conquests. It seems natural that the Muslims who had conquered all of North Africa by the year 710 (with the exception of a few cities and fortresses) would make another advance. This advance would be towards the Iberian Peninsula.

After the conquest of Al-Andalus, the Umayyads (Emeviler), who had been driven from power by the Abbasids in 750, gained new power in Al-Andalus in 756 and remained in power for 275 years, until 1031. During this long period, the Umayyad throne of Al-Andalus changed hands 19 times. Beginning with the first emir, Abd al-Rahman I (756-788), and continuing through Abd al-Rahman III (912-961), the era was characterized by rulers’ efforts to maintain harmony and create a culture of living together among different ethnic groups. These groups included Arabs, Berbers, new converts to Islam, Slavs, Christians, and Jews. New converts later outnumbered the Arab Muslims. The population also included the Spanish people, who were a mixture of Romans and Visigoths.

vocabulary.definition: A forward movement of an army.
Passed from one ruler to another.

exercises.title: A New Beginning
exercises.instructions: Read the statement. Is it true or false?
exercises.question: The Umayyads gained new power in Al-Andalus after they had been driven from power by the Abbasids.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 4: “… the Umayyads (Emeviler), who had been driven from power by the Abbasids in 750, gained new power in Al-Andalus in 756 …”

feedback.incorrect: Find 750 and 756 in paragraph 2.

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: It Seems Natural That … Would
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what “would” shows.
languageFocusExercises.question: “It seems natural that the Muslims who had conquered all of North Africa by the year 710 … would make another advance.” What does “would make” show?
options: a result that was expected from the past situation
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “It seems natural that … would + verb” presents a past development as a logical, expected step. Here, after conquering North Africa, a further advance was the expected next step.

feedback.incorrect: Is the writer asking, describing a habit, or explaining a logical next step?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Had Been, Had Conquered
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from Chapter 4.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which tense shows the earlier past?

formChoices.sentence: The Muslims who [choice] all of North Africa by the year 710 would make another advance.
The Umayyads, who [choice] from power by the Abbasids in 750, gained new power in 756.
The era [choice] by rulers’ efforts to maintain harmony.

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: The Umayyad Period

the Abbasids drove the Umayyads from power

Before 756: the conquest of all of North Africa by 710
the Abbasids drove the Umayyads from power

discussionPrompts.example: Before the club started, we had …

pages.title: Abd al-Rahman III and the Caliphate
pages.content:
The reign of Abd al-Rahman III is considered the golden age of Al-Andalus. After establishing unity within the country during the first years of his rule, he restored the state’s prestige not only within the country but also in the eyes of the Christian kingdoms. Starting in the year 951, he intensified his raids on Christian territories. After these raids, the neighboring Christian states to the north were forced to make peace with Abd al-Rahman III on the condition that they pay an annual tax. In the 10th century, partly due to the Abbasid caliphs’ loss of both political and religious influence, he viewed himself as the representative of the Islamic world and declared himself caliph in 929. Meanwhile, in 909, the Shi’i (Şii) Fatimids had also announced their caliphate in North Africa.

To compete with the Fatimids and the Byzantines in the international market, he issued gold coins. Constantinople, the Kingdom of Germany, and the Kingdom of France established diplomatic relations with Abd al-Rahman and sent envoys to his court.

To encourage harmony among the ethnic groups and reduce the influence of the former Arab aristocracy, he supported the middle class. He also promoted the development of industry and trade. Abd al-Rahman III, whose army consisted of foreign mercenaries, gave positions in the administration and the army to Christian slaves and Berbers instead of Arabs. In this way, the dominant position of the Arab nobility was weakened. On the other hand, the power of the Spaniards, who were weary of Arab nobility rather than Islamic rule, was strengthened. For example, in the mid-10th century, the Jewish Hasdây b. Şaprut served as the caliph’s court doctor during this period. Through this policy, Abd al-Rahman III united all ethnic groups into a single nation, the Andalusians.

vocabulary.definition: Official messengers sent to another ruler.

hotspots.title: Caliph in 929
hotspots.description: Abd al-Rahman III declared himself caliph in 929, partly due to the Abbasid caliphs’ loss of influence.

hotspots.title: Gold Coins
hotspots.description: To compete with the Fatimids and the Byzantines, he issued gold coins.

exercises.title: A Policy of Unity
exercises.instructions: Choose the answer that the chapter supports.
exercises.question: What was the main result of Abd al-Rahman III’s policy towards the ethnic groups?
options: He united all ethnic groups into a single nation, the Andalusians.
The Arab nobility became stronger than before.
The Christian kingdoms took control of the administration.
exercises.explanation: Chapter 5: “Through this policy, Abd al-Rahman III united all ethnic groups into a single nation, the Andalusians.”

feedback.correct: Correct. His policy created one nation, the Andalusians.
feedback.incorrect: Read the last sentence of the chapter.

languageFocusExercises.title: Notice: On the Condition That
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Read the sentence. Then choose what “on the condition that” means.
languageFocusExercises.question: “The neighboring Christian states to the north were forced to make peace with Abd al-Rahman III on the condition that they pay an annual tax.” What does it mean?
options: Peace was possible only if they paid a tax every year.
They paid the tax because they wanted peace.
They made peace, and later they decided to pay.
languageFocusExercises.explanation: “On the condition that + clause” = “only if”. The peace depended on the yearly tax. Note the base form “pay” after “that”: a formal subjunctive.

feedback.correct: Correct. It means “only if”.
feedback.incorrect: Was the tax a requirement for peace?

languageFocusExercises.title: Build: Whose, Partly Due To, Not Only … But Also
languageFocusExercises.instructions: Choose the correct form for each sentence from Chapter 5.
languageFocusExercises.question: Which form fits?

formChoices.sentence: Abd al-Rahman III, [choice] army consisted of foreign mercenaries, gave positions to Christian slaves and Berbers.
[choice] due to the Abbasid caliphs’ loss of influence, he declared himself caliph in 929.
He restored the state’s prestige not only within the country [choice] in the eyes of the Christian kingdoms.

pages.title: The Small Sultanates
pages.content:
Following the collapse of the Umayyad dynasty, the region fragmented into small emirates. This period is known as the Era of the Small Sultanates (1031–1090). During this time, the political unity of Al-Andalus disintegrated, and nearly every city in the country declared its independence. The Berbers controlled the southern coast, the Slavs controlled the eastern cities, and the Arabs and new converts to Islam came to dominate cities such as Sevilla (İşbiliye) and Toledo (Tuleytula).

Until the year 1031, the Muslims of Al-Andalus had a single state. The primary goal of the small sultanates, however, was to defend their own borders. For this reason, they even began to seek assistance from the Christian kingdoms to the north. For example, the ruling group in Tuleytula sought assistance from the Christian Kingdom of Castile to gain the upper hand. This situation led to the Muslims gradually losing power in the region. On the other hand, it provided an opportunity for the Christian kingdoms to carry out the “reconquista.” (Reconquista means taking Al-Andalus back from the Muslims.) King Ferdinand I of Castile put these sultanates under his control. The capture of Toledo in 1085, the second-largest city in Al-Andalus after Córdoba, was the heaviest blow the Christians had struck against the Muslims up to that point. The Muslims of Al-Andalus were fighting each other on various fronts and were largely unaware of the intentions of the surrounding Christian kingdoms. However, it was only with the unexpected loss of Toledo that Muslims came to realize the danger of the “reconquista.” By the mid-11th century, the Reconquista movement had taken on the character of a crusade. In this situation, they continued to exist with the support of the Berber dynasties and states in North Africa, against the Christian states.

pages.title: Christian Advances and the Fall of Granada
pages.content:
In 1230, Ferdinand III, who had united the kingdoms of Castile and León, and James I, King of Aragon, took full advantage of the situation in Al-Andalus and launched another rapid invasion. By 1236, King Ferdinand III of Castile and León had already taken control of Córdoba.

In the middle of all this chaos, the Sultanate of Granada (1231–1492) was founded in the coastal strip in the southeastern part of Al-Andalus. During this period, the only areas in Al-Andalus still under Muslim control were Granada and its surroundings. When one thinks of Al-Andalus, only Granada comes to mind. Of all the regions, only this Sultanate was able to survive against the rapid invasion carried out by the Christian kingdoms.

In 1248, the Christian King, Ferdinand III captured Sevilla. After this date, there were still many Muslims in the Christian kingdoms. They constituted distinct communities. Many were hard-working peasants in rural districts. Sometimes they were forced to dress differently and live in specific neighborhoods in the main cities. Anti-Muslim prejudice began to appear among the common people. With the marriage of Isabella, the future Queen of Castile and León, and Ferdinand II, the future King of Aragon, in 1469, which brought the two crowns together, the spread of Christianity accelerated even further, and the kingdom of Granada came to an end in 1492. Thus, the last stronghold of Islamic rule in Al-Andalus also fell.

pages.title: The Inquisition and Christianization
pages.content:
From that point on, Muslims were forced to convert to Christianity. After 1492, the policy of compulsory Christianization began to be applied to Muslims as well, in addition to Jews. The Muslims of Granada were given the choice of baptism (vaftiz: A religious ceremony performed in Christianity as a sign of accepting the Christian faith) or exile. Some of the Muslims were exiled, and new Christian communities were settled in their place. Subsequently, separate quarters were created outside the city for the remaining Muslims. They generally lived in ghetto-like neighborhoods or isolated villages. Muslims were under such intense pressure that not emigrating meant accepting Christianity.

After 1499, the Spanish government adopted a policy of “one religion” and “one nation” in Spain. To accomplish this goal, persuasion was initially used to convert Muslims to Christianity and achieved some success. However, after a while, church circles found this method to be insufficient and too slow, and they established the Inquisition (Engizisyon) in the city of Granada (1499). Many mosques were turned into churches. The Spanish administration continued to issue orders one after another to complete the process of Christianization as soon as possible. They implemented a series of bans aimed at completely discouraging people from Islam. First, slaughterhouses and butcher shops where animals were slaughtered according to Islamic rules were closed. The use of Arabic names and titles, speaking Arabic, possessing Arabic books, circumcising children, and women dressing in accordance with Islam were all prohibited. It was decided that children under the age of six would be placed in monasteries to be raised in the Christian faith. They ensured that all childbirths took place under the direct supervision of Christian midwives and that the newborn children were properly baptized. Parents were required to give their children only traditional Christian names. Religious leaders taught the Catholic faith to couples before they could get married. One of the most important social habits that set Muslims apart from the Christian societies they lived in was the use of public baths. For this reason, orders were issued to demolish these baths. It was demanded that all private and public baths be demolished, and those who disobeyed were subjected to financial penalties, primarily imprisonment.

In 1525 and 1526, similar measures were taken against Muslims in other provinces. After 1526, everyone living in Spain’s regions of Granada, Castile, Valencia, Aragon, and Catalonia was considered “officially Christian”. Thereafter, there were officially no Muslims in Spain. It is a fact that by 1525, Spain was aware of the Islamic threat to Europe by the Turkish advance towards Vienna (which was besieged in 1529).

pages.title: Ottoman Support and the Final Expulsions
pages.content:
Actually, the conquest of Constantinople (1453) was greeted with great joy in the Sultanate of Granada, just as it was in other Islamic regions. For this last Islamic state in Al-Andalus, the conquest meant the emergence of a new, powerful Muslim force to which they could look for help against the threats from Christian kingdoms. Indeed, in 1487, Emir Abu Abdullah sent an envoy to the Ottoman Sultan Bayezid II to request assistance against Ferdinand and Isabella, who were capturing their cities one by one. However, Bayezid II was unable to send the requested aid because he was occupied with his brother Cem and with the Mamluks. In response, he wrote letters to the Pope and King Ferdinand II, asking them not to oppress the Muslims of Al-Andalus. However, he achieved no result. Ten years after the fall of Granada, in 1502, the Muslims who had remained in the city sent an envoy to Bayezid II. The envoy presented the sultan with a poem expressing the religious persecution suffered by the Muslims of Andalusia and their helplessness in the face of such oppression. In response, Bayezid II sent a fleet to the Mediterranean under the command of the famous naval commander Kemal Reis. After raiding the Spanish coast, Kemal Reis rescued a group of Muslims.

Between 1609 and 1614, the Spanish expelled nearly all Muslims from the peninsula. Ahmed I, who was on the Ottoman throne at the time, was unable to take action against Spain because he was preoccupied with campaigns against both Austria and Iran, and because the Ottoman navy was not strong enough. Nevertheless, the sultan sent envoys to states such as Morocco, England, France, and Venice and requested assistance for the Muslims of Al-Andalus who wished to seek refuge in the Ottoman Empire. As a result, many Andalusians were able to reach Ottoman lands in North Africa and Istanbul.

pages.title: Society in Al-Andalus
pages.content:
In a society where the modern concept of nationalism had not yet developed, people in the Middle Ages often defined social groups through religion. So, the society of Al-Andalus consisted of two groups: Muslims and non-Muslims (gayr-i müslim). These communities included Arabs, Berbers, and local converts whose ancestors were from the Iberian population and who converted to Islam after the conquest of the region. Non-Muslims were Christians and Jews.

The number of Arabs who settled in Al-Andalus during the 8th century was around 150,000 to 200,000. It should be noted that the migration groups included not only men but also women and children. The number of Berbers was several times that of the Arabs. Therefore, it can be said that the total population of Arabs and Berbers living in Al-Andalus at the beginning of the 9th century was around half a million.

From the mid-9th century onward, the majority of the Muslim population in Al-Andalus consisted of native people who had embraced Islam.

pages.title: Christians, Jews, and Convivencia
pages.content:
Under the terms of the agreements made during the conquest, Christians were guaranteed the right to preserve their religion, places of worship, and customs, as well as the safety of their lives and property. In return, they paid the jizya (cizye: taxes collected from non-Muslim residents of an Islamic state) to the state. Those who owned land also paid land tax.

Over time, the Christian population came under the strong influence of Islamic culture. The Spaniards, too, began to use Arabic as a written and spoken language alongside their own native languages. They imitated Muslims in many aspects of daily life, such as clothing, food, and drink. For this reason, they were referred to as “Arabized.” They held important positions in various state institutions, including the military. In this way, they contributed to administrative, social, and cultural life. Thanks to their proficiency in both Arabic and Latin, as well as their close knowledge of Islamic culture, this community served as a bridge for cultural exchange between Al-Andalus and Christian Spain, and even other European countries.

Toward the end of the Visigothic period, the Jews had been completely deprived of their religious rights and enslaved. With the Islamic conquest, they were able to revive themselves as a religious community and regain the right to practice their religion freely.

When discussing Andalusian society, it is necessary to mention the term “Convivencia.” It is a Spanish word that is translated into Turkish as “living together,” “coexisting,” or “shared living.” This historical term refers to the political, social, economic, and religious interactions that took place among Muslims, Christians, and Jews in Al-Andalus between 711 and 1492. At a time when Convivencia was a way of life in Al-Andalus, nowhere else in Europe was there a comparable form of social life or coexistence. Non-Muslims, particularly Jews, lived under Islamic rule without the fear of being forced to convert. Christians and Jews had the right to participate in social, political, and economic life, with certain restrictions. This freedom allowed them to feel a sense of belonging to a shared culture while developing their own distinct communities through mutual interaction and trust. As historians say, the Islamic culture of Al-Andalus was confident and inclusive enough to include non-Islamic elements within it. Indeed, in the 10th century, the city of Córdoba in Muslim Spain, with a population of between 300,000 and 500,000 consisting of Muslims, Christians, and Jews, was Europe’s largest and most cosmopolitan metropolis.

In Andalusian society, any individual, regardless of their social background, could rise to almost any high office. The only exception was the office of head of state, which was reserved for the royal family.

Al-Andalus had become the most populous and prosperous country in Europe, particularly from the reign of Abd al-Rahman III onward. With the Great Mosque of Córdoba, whose construction was begun by Abd al-Rahman I and expanded by later rulers, as well as its other mosques, caravanserais, bathhouses, and markets, the capital city of Córdoba fascinated the entire world. The German poetess Hrotsvitha of Gandersheim called it “the ornament of the world.”

pages.title: Economic Life
pages.content:
Cities such as Sevilla, Toledo, Saragossa, Granada, and Valencia also had the same level of development. During periods of stability, the treasury’s income steadily increased. This prosperity was due to the progress made in the fields of agriculture, trade, and manufacturing. Significant progress had also been made in irrigated agriculture.

Muslims also brought crops such as rice, sugarcane, apricots, oranges, pomegranates, and cotton to Spain and grew them there as well. The manufacture of wool, cotton, and silk textiles was highly developed. It is said that there were 13,000 textile manufacturers in Córdoba alone. Products such as cotton, olives, olive oil, saffron, figs, and sugar from the coastal cities were exported to North Africa, the Byzantine Empire, and Egypt, and from there, these goods were transported to other Asian countries. Even after the complete end of Islamic rule in Al-Andalus in 1492, Muslims continued to play an influential role in the economic life of Christian Spain for some time.

pages.title: Language, Science, and Medicine
pages.content:
After the Islamic conquest, the local people in Spain, numbering 6 million, spoke Vulgar Latin, a local form of Latin from which Romance languages, including Spanish, Portuguese, and Catalan, would later develop. On the other hand, the Berbers and a very small Arab minority spoke their own languages. However, over time, there was a significant increase in the number of Arabic speakers, due both to new immigrants from the East and to marriages with local women. New converts to Islam continued to speak their native Romance dialect alongside Arabic and used both languages together in their daily lives.

Because Arabic was the official language and education was provided in that language, Arabic became the common spoken and written language of the entire Muslim population, and even of non-Muslims, beginning in the mid-9th century.

Europe rediscovered most of the works of Aristotle, Plato, Hippocrates, Galen, Ptolemy, and Euclid thanks to Arabic translations and commentaries written by Muslim scholars and philosophers. These texts, which were revived in Muslim Spain, served as a source of inspiration for Europe’s Renaissance. Knowledge flowed in one direction: from the libraries of Cairo and Baghdad to Spain, and from there to the rest of Europe. Many Christian scholars traveled south in pursuit of knowledge.

Muslims in Al-Andalus benefited from the knowledge of classical-period scholars in the fields of physiology and anatomy, and even corrected some of their errors. They also advanced the science of practical medicine and wrote significant works on the instruments used in surgery and how to use them. They also developed techniques for extracting essences from plants. They made contributions to the field of pharmacology and established pharmacies. Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi, an expert trained in the fields of medicine and chemistry, authored a thirty-volume medical encyclopedia titled et-Taṣrîf. There were many hospitals in Al-Andalus. It is known that during the Caliphate period, there were about fifty hospitals of various sizes in Córdoba alone.

pages.title: Andalusian Influence on the West
pages.content:
While Al-Andalus was establishing a sophisticated and brilliant civilization, the West was going through a period known as the “Dark Ages,” during which intellectual interests were prohibited because they were considered contrary to religion. Furthermore, the West was largely unaware of the progress made by Muslims. In the 11th century, the Crusades that were launched against both the East and Al-Andalus gave Christians the opportunity to become closely familiar with Islamic civilization. From then on, in order to gain a deeper understanding of Islamic civilization, they began translating Arabic works into their own languages. Sicily and Spain were two of the centers where the translation of scientific and philosophical works written in Arabic into Latin was most actively carried out. Muslim, Christian, and Jewish translators, at institutions where Arabic language and literature were also taught, translated numerous Arabic works on subjects such as philosophy, astronomy, mathematics, medicine, chemistry, history, geography, and literature into Latin. Thanks to these efforts, medieval Europe had the opportunity to hear about and become aware of ancient Greek philosophy, and Aristotle in particular, for the first time. Ibn Rushd’s works were taught at the University of Paris and other academic institutions. Until the 12th century, there was a belief in Europe that diseases were caused by a demon entering the human body, and that a priest had to pray to drive it out. Thanks to translations in the field of medicine, modern treatment methods began to be used.

In addition to cultural life, Al-Andalus also had a significant influence on Europe in the field of architecture. Muslims were the first to use underground canals in Spain to prevent water from evaporating and being lost. From the 12th century onward, the palaces built by certain Spanish and Portuguese kings were virtually exact replicas of the palaces in Córdoba.

The architectural works of the Muslims of Al-Andalus are not only significant for Islamic art but also of great importance for world art. Although few examples have survived to the present day, Andalusian architecture has provided Europe with some of the most beautiful examples of Islamic architecture.

pages.title: Great Works of Architecture
pages.content:
Here are a few of them:

The Great Mosque of Córdoba (Kurtuba Ulucamii): It is described as the third-largest mosque in Islamic history. Today, it has been transformed into a church and is known as the Córdoba Cathedral.

Medînetüzzehrâ Palace (Medînetüzzehrâ Sarayı): It was built during the reign of Caliph Abdurrahman III. A large number of the 4,300 columns used in the palace came from cities in Al-Andalus. Approximately one-fourth of them were brought from Carthage, Tunis, Constantinople, and Frankish territories.

Alhambra Palace (Elhamrâ Sarayı): The palace in Gırnata (Granada) is of great importance not only for Andalusian architecture but also for Islamic art as a whole. It is described with the adjective el-hamrâ, meaning “red,” because of the reddish color of the clay used in its construction. Although its history as a military fortress dates back to the 9th century, its famous courtyards with pools, decorated halls, and royal palaces were built in the 13th and 14th centuries.

Alcazar Palace (İşbiliye/Seville, el-Kasr - Alkazar Sarayı): The Alcazar of Seville, whose name comes from the Arabic al-qasr, is a royal palace in the heart of Seville (İşbiliye). The palace has been redecorated many times from the 11th century to modern times. The building was constructed by Muslim carpenters, and these craftsmen were brought from Tuleytula.

pages.title: Learning and Intellectual Legacy
pages.content:
In summary, the following examples highlight the extraordinary nature of Andalusian civilization in the circumstances of its time.

Thanks to Caliph Hakem II’s (961–976) passion for learning, his library had more than 400,000 volumes.

Before the influence of Islamic medicine (tıp bilimi), medicine in Europe was in its most primitive stages. Even in the 1200s, European hospitals remained far behind Muslim hospital standards. Ibn Sînâ’s (d. 1037) work al-Qanun fi’t-Tibb, described as “the masterpiece of Arabic,” was translated into Latin in the 12th century. It has been published in numerous editions, including one in Hebrew. These editions were printed 16 times in the 15th century, twice in the 16th century, and many times in the 17th century. This work served as the sole textbook taught in all European universities offering medical education at least until the end of the 16th century. This translation was done in the Andalusian city of Toledo.

Another important scholar of Al-Andalus was Ibn Hazm (994–1064). It is said that during his seventy-year life, Ibn Hazm wrote approximately 400 volumes (80,000 pages) of works, about three dozen of which have survived to the present day, primarily in the fields of fiqh and the history of religions.

Hayy ibn Yaqzan, written by the Andalusian philosopher and physician Ibn Tufayl, is considered a literary and philosophical masterpiece in its own right. In fact, various researchers have noted that this work served as a source of inspiration, particularly for Daniel Defoe’s Robinson Crusoe.

pages.title: Seville and a Lasting Legacy
pages.content: As mentioned above, the Christian King, Ferdinand III of Castile captured Seville in 1248. In the words of the Spanish cultural historian Americo Castro, “When the victorious (Christian) armies saw Seville in 1248, they could not hide their amazement. Because in the fields of art, economic development, civil order, technology, and scientific and literary production, Christians had never had anything comparable to this.”

Accepted fact: It is known that during the conquest …
